## Paper

## Abstract

Sustainable batteries necessitate high-performance hard carbon negative electrodes derived from abundant biomass. However, realizing their full potential is significantly limited by the inherent diversity of biomass feedstocks, the intricate control over carbonization and resulting microstructures, and the complex interplay between processing, structure, and electrochemical performance. Here, we introduce “intelligent carbonization”, a strategy integrating programmable Joule heating (1000-2000 °C, 10-60 s) with machine learning to substantially accelerate the discovery and optimization of biomass-derived hard carbons. By mapping over 1000 synthetic pathways and decoding the multidimensional feature space, we reveal a performance-correlated factor that serves as a crucial predictor of capacity, complementing conventional graphitic descriptors (in-plane crystallite size/ interlayer spacing). By a minimal energy input (0.1 kWh g-1), our strategy converts biochar into advanced hard carbon delivering 369 mAh g-1 reversible capacity, high rate capability, and improved cycling stability (>5000 cycles at a specific current of 3 A g-1). This data-centric approach allows low-cost and intelligent manufacturing of diverse biomass resources into performance-unified hard carbon negative electrodes, thereby paving the way for practical and large-scale biomass valorization towards sustainable energy storage solutions.

---

## Introduction

With an annual global production exceeding 220 billion oven dry tonne (odt) (or 4500EJ)1, biomass stands as an exceptionally vast, renewable, and ubiquitous reservoir, offering considerable potential for carbon-neutral product development2-5. The conversion of biomass into sustainable hard carbon (HC) negative electrodes is critical for fast charging lithium-ion batteries and particularly industrializing sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), which target large-scale grid storage demanding vast material supply and costs below $50 per kWh6. This dual role in energy storage and resource valorization underscores the importance of HC in advancing both renewable energy technologies and sustainable industrial practices. However, the complex and variable nature of biomass precursors makes it difficult to produce HC with consistent and predictable properties7-9, typically scattering from 150-300 mAh g-1, posing a significant barrier to industrial-scale manufacturing. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of carbonization and the unclear structure-property relationship hinders the rational design of HC from diverse biomass resources. Addressing these fundamental challenges is key to unlocking the full potential of biomass in next-generation energy storage.

Conventionally, HCs are produced via a two-step carbonization: 1) a low-temperature pyrolysis (~700°C) to yield the biochar, and 2) a high-temperature carbonization10-15 (e.g., 1400–1500°C for >2 hours) to tailor the graphitic microstructure of biochar into HC. While the biochar is abundant and cheap, the simple pyrolysis leads to premature microstructures and unsatisfactory performance (<200 mAh g-1)16, 17 (Fig. 1a). The latter carbonization stage, crucial for forming HC, is notably energy-intensive and incurs significant carbon emissions. Importantly, after this prolonged carbonization, HCs possess a complex microstructure with randomly oriented graphitic microcrystals, amorphous regions, and nanopores18-20, leading to variations in microstructure and performance across different biomass sources. For example, the rigid, lignin-containing frameworks of wood21, 22 and bamboo23 tend to produce carbons with robust, hierarchical pore systems; In contrast, the highly crystalline and pure cellulose from cotton11 is more conducive to forming well-ordered graphitic domains, translating into differing electrochemical behaviors (134~300 mAh g-1)24, 25. Moreover, the convoluted evolution of multiple structural parameters—such as graphitic microcrystal size, interlayer spacing, and porosity—is inherent to conventional carbonization26-30, posing a profound challenge of elucidating their structure-performance relationships. Consequently, the development of HC has been largely confined to an empirical, trial-and-error paradigm. While targeted synthetic strategies have provided initial insights correlating structure with reversible capacity, a quantitative and predictive understanding remains elusive31. In sum, developing biomass-derived HCs is hindered by three major challenges: 1) the energy-intensive carbonization process; 2) biomass diversity and performance variations; and 3) complex process-structure-property correlations for understanding and rational design.

Accordingly, establishing a paradigm for efficient, predictable, and genuinely sustainable manufacturing of HC with consistent performance is critical to advancing SIB technology. Herein, by integrating energy-efficient programmable Joule heating32, 33 (PJH) with machine learning (ML), our intelligent carbonization strategy unveils a critical capacity descriptor that unlocks the sustainable production of consistent HC from diverse biomass (Fig. 1b). The centerpiece of our discovery is a performance-correlated factor (PCF), derived from X-ray diffraction (XRD) data, which critically supplements traditional metrics like La and d002, together enabling a predictive model with greater accuracy for electrochemical capacity. This allows us to yield digital HC (Dig-HC) that exhibits a capacity of 369 mAh g⁻¹ (at 0.2 C, 1 C=300 mA g-1), more than doubling the biochar’s capacity of 150 mAh g⁻¹ (Fig. 1c), while also showing strong rate performance (280 mAh g⁻¹ at 10 C) and >5000 cycle stability. Critically, this improvement is achieved by PJH synthesis in an exceptionally energy-efficient manner34, consuming merely 0.1 kWh g-1 of electrical energy (~6% compared to biochar production). Our approach enables the production of a sustainable and high-performing Dig-HC from low cost biochar with an estimated production cost of ~$6,000 per ton—less than reported HCs (Fig. 1d). Leveraging this strategy, we demonstrate a full life sustainability pathway for HC negative electrodes: from renewable biomass, through an energy-efficient electrified carbonization process, to a durable high-performance HC negative electrode that enables a more resilient and sustainable energy future.

---

## Results

Synthesis and process optimization guided by machine learning.
While ML holds significant promise for materials science35-37, its application to HCs has been constrained by the bottleneck of slow, traditional experimental data acquisition. Specifically, while the initial synthesis of biochar from biomass via low temperature pyrolysis (T1: 600-800 °C, t1: 1-2 h) (Supplementary Fig. 1) is a rapid, high-throughput, and energetically favorable process, its conversion into HC is hampered by a lengthy and energy-intensive high-temperature carbonization (1400-1600 °C) that requires over 500 minutes. Our PJH carbonization strategy circumvents this limitation and completes the transformation from biochar to HC in under one minute (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Table 1). Compared to conventional carbonization, our method reduces the processing time by 500 times while requiring only 0.1 kWh g-1 of the energy input (Fig. 2b), with the detailed calculation shown in Supplementary Note 1. Despite the sub-minute processing time, XRD analysis confirmed that this rapid synthesis method does not sacrifice structural quality (Fig. 2c). The PJH treatment was sufficient to increase the in-plane crystallite size (La) from 2.184 to 2.64 nm while its transient nature effectively preserves a favorable interlayer spacing (0.371 nm) (d002) (conventional carbonization is 0.361 nm) and stacking height (Lc) a structural outcome that is beneficial for rapid Na⁺ intercalation and high rate performances38.

The four heating parameters create a vast design space (T1: 300-900 °C; t1: 60-120 min; T2: 1000-2200 °C; t2: 1-60 s) wherein material performance is highly sensitive to process variations, resulting in a diverse range of performances: e.g., capacity 100-300 mAh g-1, initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) 30-80% (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 2). Therefore, a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model coupled with an active learning strategy using an Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function39-41 (Supplementary Fig. 3) was applied to accelerate optimization of capacity and ICE of Dig-HC under four process parameters: pyrolysis (T1, t1) and PJH carbonization (T2, t2). Our initial analysis revealed moderate and comparable linear correlations for all four process parameters, while a strong linear correlation (R = 0.94) was identified between ICE and capacity (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 4). This simplifies our approach, whereby the dual-objective optimization was reformulated into a more parsimonious single-objective problem targeting only capacity. Our predictive surrogate model yielded a training R2 of 0.96, demonstrating its high fidelity in representing the performance landscape defined by the chosen data (Fig. 2f).

Our optimization strategy commenced with an analysis of the initial dataset, which identified that the PJH carbonization conditions of T2 >1800 °C are associated with higher capacity in our dataset. We initially fixed the PJH carbonization parameter (T2=1800 ℃; t2=40 s) to focus on optimizing the pyrolysis conditions (T1 and t1) (Supplementary Fig. 5). Upon mapping the parameter space (T1; t1) with the GPR model, we identified T₁=800 °C and t₁=1.5 h as the optimal condition for pyrolysis, considering its higher predicted capacity, lower energy consumption, and alignment with findings in the literatures11, 42, 43. Following T1, t1 determination, the PJH process parameters T2 and t2 were identified as an optimal second-stage temperature (T₂) of 1800 °C and the PJH duration (t2) of 40 s (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Fig. 6). After one iteration, the final model’s R² remains above 0.9, showing the stability of GPR model. The whole parameter space spanned pyrolysis and PJH carbonization, with predictions across 1,453 generated parameter combinations within this extensive matrix (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 7) facilitating later ML-guided optimization and intelligent manufacturing.

Electrochemical properties
To elucidate the advantages of our ML-guided intelligent carbonization, the resulting Dig-HC was compared against biochar and commercial Kuraray HC, showing higher sodium storage capabilities over the reference carbon negative electrodes. In initial charge-discharge cycles in ester-based electrolytes (Fig. 3a), Dig-HC achieved a high reversible capacity of 369 mAh g-1 and an ICE of 79%, exceeding precursor biochar (150 mAh g-1, 35% ICE) and commercial Kuraray HC (290 mAh g-1, 75% ICE)44, 45. To intuitively analyze the origins of its enhanced capacity, we performed a segmental analysis of the discharge profile (Fig. 3b), which revealed a dominant capacity contribution from the intermediate voltage stage in Dig-HC, delivering a 233.58 mAh g⁻¹. Furthermore, Dig-HC maintains 94.3% capacity retention at 0.2 C after 100 cycles (Fig. 3c), comparing favourably with Kuraray HC and biochar. According to the Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) profiles in Fig. 3d, Dig-HC exhibited a lower charge-transfer resistance (Rct) of only 23.67 Ω than that of biochar (52.24 Ω) and Kuraray HC (29.98 Ω), indicating an improved diffusion kinetics of Na ions (Supplementary Fig. 8, Supplementary Table 3). Additionally, the Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) analysis shows that Dig-HC has a larger integrated area, indicating a higher reversible capacity, as well as increased peak currents, which correspond to faster reaction kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 9).

The rate capability of Dig-HC was tested in an ether-based electrolyte to assess its performance robustness across different electrolyte systems. Fig. 3e summarizes Dig-HC alongside biochar, Kuraray HC, and representative literatures31, 42, 44-48 HCs under different specific currents. Dig-HC delivers 350 mAh g-1 at 0.2 C and 280 mAh g-1 at 10 C, surpassing biochar, Kuraray HC (Supplementary Table 4). Moreover, in the more challenging carbonate-based electrolyte system, Dig‑HC delivered ~80 mAh g-1 at 10 C—higher than biochar and Kuraray HC (<50 mAh g-1) (Supplementary Fig. 10). This further demonstrates the broad electrolyte-system compatibility of Dig‑HC enabled by our intelligent carbonization strategy. It clearly demonstrates that the contribution from fast, surface-controlled capacitive processes progressively increases from 45% at 0.1 mV s-1 to a dominant 72% at 1.0 mV s-1. This increasing dominance of non-diffusion-limited capacitive charge storage is the fundamental reason for the material’s strong high-rate performance (Supplementary Fig. 11). Regarding low-temperature performance, Dig-HC stabilized at 235.3 mAh g-1 and retained 97% of this capacity after 100 cycles at -40℃. It surpassed Kuraray HC, which delivered a capacity of 225.7 mAh g-1 before it short-circuited at the 17th cycle under identical conditions (Fig. 3f). Overall, Dig-HC demonstrated a robust electrochemical performance across a wide temperature range from -40 to 25°C (Supplementary Fig. 12). Even when the charging-discharging rate increased to 10 C, Dig-HC delivered 280 mAh g-1 and maintained 87.4% capacity retention after 5000 cycles, demonstrating enhanced stability relative to biochar (retained 62.4% after 4000 cycles) and Kuraray HC (short-circuited at 3000th) (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, when used as an negative electrode material in lithium‑ion batteries, Dig‑HC delivers a higher capacity (385 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g-1) than commercially reported graphite49 (372 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g-1). It also exhibits better rate capability, retaining approximately 141 mAh g−1 under a high specific current of 1 A g-1 (Supplementary Fig. 13).

Elucidation of structure-property relationships.
Despite achieving optimized Dig-HC performance, a comprehensive, predictive understanding of HC’s intricate structure-property relationships remains largely elusive. We selected XRD as the primary characterization tool, as it provides essential microstructural parameters (e.g., interlayer spacing d002, La, and Lc), with the detailed calculation shown in Supplementary Note 2, which are widely recognized as key factors influencing the performance of HCs (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 14). Moreover, the rapid, cost-effective, and highly reproducible nature of XRD makes it suited for generating the large datasets necessary to train a robust ML model and later industrial adoption. Conversely, techniques like high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) are ill-suited for large-scale feedback due to their localized sampling, complex preparation, and high operational costs. Moreover, relying on precursor characterization is infeasible, as the substantial evolution in phase and functional groups during carbonization severs the direct link between the starting material’s properties and the final negative electrode performance.

It should also be noted that the integrated areas of the (002) (i.e., A002) and (100) (i.e., A100) XRD peaks—which quantify c-axis stacking and in-plane graphitic order, respectively—are critical structural descriptors that are frequently ignored (Fig. 4b). Seven indices were chosen for subsequent analysis, including six physically meaningful features of d002, the interplanar spacing of the graphite (100) planes d100, Lₐ, Lc, A100, and A002 (Supplementary Table 5) and capacity. To bolster model robustness, extensive literature data on HC structural parameters were compiled (Supplementary Table 6) with our experimental data. Meanwhile, the range of both input structural indices and output capacities (Fig. 4c) is expansive, which underpins the development of a generalizable model capable of robustly identifying the optimal hard carbon structure.

By leveraging the automated feature extraction capabilities of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) (Supplementary Fig. 14), our model autonomously constructed four interaction features (A100/(A100+A002), N, A100+A002, and A100/A002) from the six primary descriptors, where A100/(A100+A002), named performance correlated factor (PCF), exhibits the strongest positive correlation with capacity (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 16,17). It reflects the relative contribution of in-plane ordering to the overall degree of order in HC (Supplementary Fig. 18). In other words, it serves as a mesoscale morphological descriptor rather than a direct crystallographic parameter50, 51. Built upon this enriched feature set, the surrogated predictive model demonstrated high accuracy, with R² values surpassing 0.94 on both the training and testing sets (Fig. 4e).

We then employed Shapley additive explanations52 (SHAP) to uncover the intricate, non-linear structure-property relationships within the MLP model, which reveals that the engineered feature, PCF, is the most dominant positive driver (Fig. 4f). It represents the fraction of in-plane graphitic ordering relative to the total crystalline content. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that a combination of a larger La and a smaller Lc is advantageous for Na⁺ storage, which is consistent with our linear correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. 19). It also clarified the nuanced role of d002, whose positive impact at a localized sweet spot (0.37-0.38 nm), thus reconciling our findings with the broader literature14, 20, 47. SHAP dependence plots (Supplementary Fig. 20) shows PCF and La have strong positive monotonic effects on predicted capacity, while d002 contributes positively within a narrow 0.37–0.39 nm window. Feature interactions indicate that enlarging d002 simply is ineffective, high capacity also demands a large La, and a high PCF. The PJH process notably co-optimizes PCF and La while pinning d002 in the optimal range, enabling the improved sodium storage.

To further corroborate the ML-elucidated structure-property relationships, a suite of additional characterization techniques was employed to compare Dig-HC and biochar samples (Supplementary Table 7, 8). While both samples displayed broad (002) and (100) graphitic carbon peaks in XRD, Dig-HC’s peaks were more intense and exhibited larger integrated areas53. Comparative analysis (Fig. 4g) showed Dig-HC possessed an increased PCF of 0.2 and a larger La of 2.64 nm relative to biochar, signifying a more ordered in-plane structure with larger graphitic domains. This structural enhancement is directly responsible for the increase in its plateau capacity, as it allows for more facile Na⁺ intercalation and pore-filling54. Critically, despite the intense thermal shock, the transient PJH treatment effectively preserved an interlayer spacing of 0.37-0.38 nm in Dig-HC, a range optimal for facilitating efficient Na⁺ intercalation55. Collectively, the intelligent carbonization strategy simultaneously promotes the lateral growth of short-range ordered graphitic domains (enhancing La and PCF) while suppressing their c-axis stacking (maintaining a larger d002 and a smaller Lc), a process wherein the curled edges of the microcrystals form abundant closed pores. These distinct structural attributes affirm that an engineered graphitic microcrystalline framework promotes high-performance sodium storage.

In addition, N2 adsorption-desorption analysis (Supplementary Fig. 21) revealed that the PJH process dramatically reduced the specific surface area (SSA) from 82.48 m2 g-1 for the biochar to 5.48 m2 g-1 for Dig-HC. This reduction is anticipated to curtail parasitic electrolyte reactions, thereby enhancing ICE and reversibility25. Concurrently, the average open pore diameters of biochar and Dig-HC are 2.2 nm and 9.14 nm, respectively. This observation is likely ascribed to the metastable, kinetically-dominated PJH process (< 1 min at ultrahigh temperature). During the rapid heating ramp Lc initially decreased (from 1.05 to 0.75 nm), while a 40 s dwell at peak temperature promoted recrystallization and an increase in La (from 2.18 to 2.64 nm). The subsequent rapid quench caused the thin, laterally large graphite microcrystalline platelets to curl, leading to the formation of larger closed pores. Together, these time-dependent kinetic effects during PJH explain the observed evolution of microstructure and porosity38, 56. Similar rapid synthesis techniques likewise show that employing rapid heating and cooling profiles can produce hard carbon with fewer defects and a richer, more diversified pore structure56. Further Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS)analysis (Supplementary Fig. 22, 23) elucidated a distinct shoulder in the scattering profile of Dig-HC (the scattering vector (q) range of 0.1-0.4 Å⁻¹, absent in biochar). This indicates the formation of larger, more well-defined closed pores, with the average size increasing from ~0.67 nm to 4.15 nm (Fig. 4h). Such developed closed porosity is believed to facilitate Na cluster formation, contributing to the low-voltage plateau capacity and concurrently bolstering ICE. Meanwhile, the first-cycle CV curves further indicate that this structure is more compatible with ether-based electrolytes than with ester-based ones , exhibiting sharper and higher peak currents and fewer side reactions, which facilitate the formation of a stable solid electrolyte interphase (Supplementary Fig. 24). Although morphological analysis by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) indicated no discernible differences among the three samples (Supplementary Fig. 25), HRTEM provided direct visual evidence for the structural evolution from biochar to Dig-HC (Fig. 4i, 4j, Supplementary Fig. 26). Dig-HC exhibited a more ordered graphitic microcrystalline architecture and a distinct internal porosity, indicating a higher degree of local graphitic ordering. Compared to biochar, Dig-HC possesses larger enclosed nanopores formed by the curling of short-range ordered graphitic micro-crystallites.

Raman spectroscopy57 (Supplementary Fig. 27) indicated that higher PJH temperatures lead to both a slight decrease in the ID/IG ratio (enhanced ordering) and an increase in capacity. According to the X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) results (Supplementary Table 9), C 1s spectra for Dig-HC revealed a higher proportion of C=C bonds (~284.8 eV), while O 1s spectra showed decreased C=O content (~532.3 eV) (Supplementary Fig. 28). This latter observation signifies effective impurity removal and suggests an increased sp3-carbon proportion as well as a more ordered carbon structure, which is considered beneficial for Na storage58. These results are consistent with the XRD and Raman data, further demonstrating the important role of PCF parameters for the enhanced battery performance.

Practicality and Outlook.
An intelligent manufacturing process (Fig. 5a, Supplementary Table 10, Supplementary Fig. 29) is proposed for highly efficient production of Dig-HC with high performance in real time based on the combination of the transient PJH method, the in-situ XRD characterization, and ML algorithm. In this workflow, the sub-minute (<1 min) PJH platform performs high-throughput synthesis. Concurrently, in-situ XRD extracts key structural features (e.g., PCF, La, d002). Based on our pre-established process-structure-property model, the ML algorithm uses these features to predict battery’s performance, perform inverse design, and generate recommendations for optimal process parameters. These recommendations are immediately fed back to the PJH process, enabling precise and rapid tuning of the HC’s structural features to meet target performance. Ultimately, this intelligent production approach not only replaces labor-intensive battery assembly and testing with rapid, data-driven XRD analysis and ML prediction but also establishes an efficient paradigm for the intelligent manufacturing of advanced HC negative electrodes with consistent and stable performance (Fig. 5b). Dig-HC not only shows enhanced performance than the conventional HC (Con-HC) in terms of capacity, rate, and cycling, but also achieves substantial gains in energy and time efficiency with a much smaller carbon footprint59. We used COMSOL Multiphysics to simulate the temperature distribution of a 100 cm × 60 cm heated substrate. The central processing region exhibits a highly uniform temperature field (Supplementary Fig. 30, Supplementary Table 11), consistent with the stable material quality observed at scale (Supplementary Fig. 31).

The adaptive control feature of our intelligent manufacturing process can be engineered to address the diversity of biomass precursors. For example, despite the profound structural differences between precursors—ranging from highly crystalline cotton (90% cellulose) and complex lignocellulosic peanut shells (45% cellulose) to glucose—our intelligent manufacturing successfully identified a robust optimization route for each, yielding HC capacities in the range of 340-370 mAh g⁻¹ (at 0.2 C) (Fig. 5c). On the other hand, our strategy can effectively achieve product and performance uniformity even from heterogeneous feedstocks. By manipulating the PJH parameters independently, Dig-HCs derived from the three above precursors exhibit a similar microstructure, evidenced by a convergence in their PCF from XRD analysis (Supplementary Fig. 32). As a result, our optimization strategy can consistently deliver consistent and high-capacity HCs stabilized at 340 mAh g-1, regardless of precursor origin (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Table 12). Furthermore, when substituting the input variables with the fundamental lignocellulosic ratios (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin), our intelligent carbonization strategy successfully converts these diverse compositions into performance-unified HC negative electrodes (330 mAh g-1) through iterative optimization (Supplementary Table 13, Supplementary Fig. 33). Significantly, the intelligent carbonization establishes a transferable paradigm for materials discovery. By leveraging transfer learning60 to freeze universal structure-property layers, the model can be rapidly adapted to updated multi-ion systems with minimal experimental data, enabling the efficient inverse design of bespoke materials for next-generation energy storage.

We performed a comprehensive techno-economic analysis (TEA) and life cycle assessment (LCA) of our intelligent carbonization strategy (Fig. 5e, 5f, Supplementary Table 14). Detailed analysis procedures, assumptions, and input parameters are described in Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Note 4. Specifically, our strategy reduces the carbon footprint from the carbonization stage by a factor of 14 and the overall costs by a factor of 30 relative to conventional carbonization. This leads to a 16-fold reduction in overall lifecycle emissions and an 8-fold reduction in total development cost, establishing a scalable blueprint where improved performance is achieved in concert with, not at the expense of, economic and ecological sustainability. From a life-cycle perspective, we establish a holistic and sustainable life cycle for advanced HC from biomass (Fig. 5g). The cycle starts with abundant and renewable biomass, which serves as a carbon-neutral and sustainable feedstock. This raw material is then transformed via our intelligent carbonization strategy, where energy-efficient and electrified PJH33 is guided by ML to minimize energy waste and consumption in producing high-performance and low-cost HC negative electrodes. The resulting HC then enables durable and long-life SIBs for sustainable energy storage applications. This sustainable cycle consists of renewable materials, electrified synthesis, and clean energy storage, representing a holistic, full-lifecycle approach to sustainable energy technology.

## Methods

Chemical and materials.
Cellulose powder (97%, ≤25 μm, Innochem, A06413, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ) was used as precursor. Cotton (degreased absorbent cotton; Labshark; purity 99%), peanut shells (purchased from Tan’ernuo; purity 90%), and glucose (Macklin; purity 98%) were used as biomass precursors. Acetylene black, polyvinylidene fluoride (Solef, PVDF 5130, DP = (1.0-1.2) × 106), Cu collector (purity ≥ 99.9%, thickness 9 μm) and CR2032 cell cases were acquired from Shenzhen Ke Jing Zhi Da Technology Co., Ltd. N-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP, purity ≥ 99%) were purchased from Aladdin. Organic electrolyte (ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate (EC/DMC = 1:1 by volume) or diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DIGLYME)) were purchased from DoDoChem. All reagents were used as received without further purification.

Material preparation.
All HC samples were prepared from cellulose pyrolysis (Innochem, microcrystalline powder) or complex biomass precursors (cotton, peanut shell, glucose) in two steps. Both steps of the heat treatment were conducted in an argon atmosphere. During the first stage of pyrolysis in a tubular furnace, cellulose powder was heated from room temperature to 800 °C at a rate of 5 °C min-1 and held at 800 °C (T1) for 90 minutes (t1) before cooling naturally to room temperature to form biochar. In the second step, PJH carbonization was performed using the programmable Joule heating method, rapidly heating to 1800 °C (T2) within 1 second and maintaining it for 20 s (t2), repeating this operation once. The HC material obtained by this method was named Dig-HC.

Materials characterization.
Scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30) were used to obtain information on microstructure. The phase was identified by XRD-7000 (Shimadzu, Japan) with a scanning rate of 10 ° min-1 (Cu K radiation, λ =1.5406 Å). Raman spectra were obtained by a WITEC alpha-300R, Germany. Pore distribution was tested by Xeuss 3.0 UHR, Xenocs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) was employed to analyze the chemical state of C, O and N.

Electrochemical measurements.
The negative electrode slurry was prepared by mixing 80 wt.% active material (Dig-HC) with 10 wt% acetylene black (Denka black, Denki Kagaku Kogyo; Average particle size was 20-40 nm) and 10 wt.% PVDF in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). The amount of NMP was fixed at 5 μL per mg of active material (e.g., 400 μL NMP for 80 mg active material). The mixture was stirred for 12 h at 26 ± 1 °C, and the resulting slurry was coated onto a single-sided copper foil current collector (purity 99.9%, thickness 9 μm) using an automatic coating machine. The prepared electrodes were dried overnight under vacuum at 120°C. The subsequent product was then cut into electrode sheets with a diameter of 12 mm using a disk cutter (Shenzhen Kejing, MSK-T10), and the loading mass of the active material was approximately 1-2 mg cm-2. A 0.4 mm sodium metal (diameter 14 mm, DoDoChem, stored in an Ar-filled glovebox (H2O and O2 levels both < 0.01 ppm) for no longer than one month before use) as the counter electrode and glass fiber (Whatman GF/A CAT. No.1820-090, diameter 16 mm, thickness 260 μm, pore size 1.6 μm, porosity 40%) as the separator, within an argon-filled glove box. The 1 M NaPF6 solution in ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate (EC/DMC = 1:1 by volume) or diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DIGLYME) was used as the electrolyte, and the amount is 120 μL. Charge and discharge measurements were conducted in a climatic chamber (25 ± 0.5 °C) using a Neware multi-channel battery testing system (CS3104).

In cycling test, the cells were tested from 2 V to 0.004 V with a specific current of 0.2 C or 10 C. In the low-temperature half-cell test, the temperature was set to -20 °C or -40 ℃, while all other conditions remained unchanged. CV curves were obtained with a scan rate of 0.1 mV s-1. The potentiostatic EIS measurement was conducted using an electrochemical workstation (CS6, Corrtest, Wuhan) in the frequency range 0.1 Hz-100 kHz with a signal amplitude of 5 mV. A total of 50 points were collected within the test frequency range. A quasi-stationary potential was applied for 600 s before carrying out the EIS measurement.

Machine learning models.
To quantitatively map the synthesis-structure-property relationships of the hard carbon, we developed a suite of machine learning models. First, a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model was established to predict the final specific capacity directly from four heating process parameters (designated T1, t1, T2, and t2). In parallel, a MLP, incorporating Dropout and L2 regularization and optimized via grid search, was trained to model the link between six key structural parameters and specific capacity.

Our GPR model was constructed using a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel as the covariance function, a standard and robust choice for modeling smooth response surfaces. The specific kernel was set as kernel = 1.0 * RBF (length scale=1.0); The primary advantages of the RBF kernel are its versatility and smoothness. As a stationary kernel, it is highly effective at capturing the smooth, non-linear response surfaces characteristic of materials properties, such as the capacity in this work. Its non-parametric nature allows it to flexibly fit complex functional forms without requiring a priori assumptions about the underlying mathematical relationship.

Our optimization strategy uses a closed-loop active learning workflow that couples data acquisition, feature extraction and surrogate modelling with experimental validation. The key step is the choice of the next experimental candidate. To make this decision, the algorithm updates the surrogate after each measurement and uses both the predicted performance and its associated uncertainty to steer the search—prioritizing promising regions while still probing less-sampled areas where uncertainty is higher. To implement this, we utilized Bayesian Optimization coupled with an Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function. The EI metric is particularly effective for this dual-objective task as it simultaneously evaluates the probability of outperforming the current best result and the potential magnitude of that improvement. The EI is calculated as follows:

EI(x) = (μ(x) - f(x+)) Φ(Z) + σ(x) φ(Z) (1)

where μ(x) and σ(x) correspond to the predictive mean and standard deviation of the GPR model. f(x+) indicates the highest capacity observed to date. ξ is a tuning parameter that governs the balance between exploitation and exploration, for which we adopted the recommended default value of 0.01. Z = (μ(x) - f(x+) - ξ) / σ(x). Φ and φ represent the standard normal Cumulative Distribution Function and Probability Density Function, respectively. During each active learning loop, the model targets the candidate x* that maximizes the EI function, thereby guiding the experimental pathway toward the most promising unobserved regions.

Small-angle X-ray scattering.
SAXS measurements were carried out using a Xenocs Xeuss 3.0 system equipped with a Cu Kα micro-focus X-ray source (λ = 1.5419 Å) operated at 30 W. The scattering signals were recorded by a Pilatus 3R 300K detector (Dectris) with a pixel size of 172 μm. The sample-to-detector distance was set to approximately 200 mm to cover the scattering vector (q) range of interest (0.001–1.0 Å-1). Samples were loaded into capillaries for transmission mode acquisition. The 2D scattering patterns were azimuthally integrated to 1D curves, followed by background subtraction and transmission correction using the instrument’s standard software package.

As defined in the manuscript, PCF is extracted from the XRD patterns of hard carbon as the ratio between the integrated area of the (100) peak and the total integrated peak area (Fig. R3a), and therefore functions as a mesoscopic morphological descriptor.
Physically, PCF statistically quantifies the relative dominance of in-plane graphitic ordering (2D aromatic continuity) versus c-axis stacking (3D graphitization) within the hard carbon matrix, a feature identified in previous work (Adv. Phys. 1986, 35, 317-374). A higher PCF indicates microstructures with laterally well-developed aromatic sheets (Nature 2024, 634, 80–84) that remain thinly stacked and turbostratic—reflecting a preference for 2D sheet extension over 3D stacking (Fig. R3b, c).

Differences with traditional descriptors: Traditional descriptors such as La, Lc and d002 are crystallographic constants obtained from peak broadening and positions in XRD; they describe the absolute crystallite dimensions (La: lateral domain size; Lc: stacking height) (Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, e2302613). In contrast, PCF is not a size metric; It is an engineering feature derived from integrated intensities that captures the relative extent of in-plane order within the total crystalline ordering, thereby reflecting material organization and the degree of turbostratic disorder.

Details of EI function: Our active learning loop was designed to identify the optimal performance within a minimal number of experimental iterations (in this case, only one iterations). The critical step is the selection of the “next-best” experimental point. To achieve this, we employed a Bayesian Optimization sampling strategy. Specifically, we used the Expected Improvement (EI) as the acquisition function to guide the selection. The primary advantage of the EI function is its inherent ability to optimally balance the trade-off between exploitation and exploration. The EI is calculated as follows:
EI(x)=(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)Φ(Z)+σ(x)φ(Z)
where, μ(x) and σ(x) are the predictive mean and predictive standard deviation, respectively, of the GPR model at pointx. f(x+) is the best value observed among all experiments conducted so far. ξ is a tuning parameter that governs the balance between exploitation and exploration, for which we adopted the recommended default value of 0.01. Z =(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)/σ(x). Φ() and φ() are the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) and the Probability Density Function (PDF) of the standard normal distribution, respectively.
In each iteration of the active learning loop, we select the process parametersx* =argmaxEI(x)
that maximize the EI value as the next point for experimental validation.

It is a big challenge to establish the quantitative conversion relationship between them. The specific advantages and limitations are as follows.
1. XRD (PCF): It serves as a bulk characterization technique that provides statistically averaged structural information over a large sample volume (mm3 scale), mitigating bias from local heterogeneity (Energy & Environmental Science, 2024, 17, 8189-8197). Crucially, the PCF is a mesoscopic morphological descriptor. It captures the relative dominance of in-plane ordering (La) versus c-axis stacking (Lc), effectively describing the unique “large sheet, thin stack” morphology of PJH-treated carbon. It is less sensitive to the chemical states of surface functional groups compared to XPS, which is not important to the sodium storage (Fig. R13a).
2. Raman (ID/IG): Raman spectroscopy is exceptionally sensitive to short-range disorder and defects (e.g., edge sites, vacancies) via phonon vibration modes (μm scale). Furthermore, the ID/IG ratio often exhibits similarity in HCs (Energy & Environmental Science 2024, 17, 1387-1396), limiting its quantitative linearity for ML modeling (Fig. R13b).
3. XPS (C=C %): XPS provides precise quantitative analysis of chemical bonding states (e.g., sp2 vs. sp3) and heteroatom content. It is strictly a surface-sensitive technique (probing depth < 10 nm) (Adv Mater, 2025, e11632). Since sodium storage is primarily a bulk phenomenon occurring in internal pores and layers, surface chemistry alone cannot fully predict the capacity (Fig. R13c).
Establishing a mathematical conversion between these metrics is scientifically challenging because they measure fundamentally different physical phenomena: long-range lattice diffraction (XRD) vs. short-range phonon vibration (Raman) vs. surface photoelectron emission (XPS). However, these metrics are qualitatively consistent and mutually corroborating (Fig. R13). The PJH treatment leads to a simultaneous increase in the PCF (indicating extended in-plane order), a higher proportion of C=C bonds (indicating defect healing), and a slight decrease in the ID/IG ratio (indicating reduced disorder).

Technol. Adv. Mater 2023, 24, 2). The specific kernel was set as kernel = 1.0 * RBF (length scale=1.0); The primary advantages of the RBF kernel are its versatility and smoothness. As a stationary kernel, it is highly effective at capturing the smooth, non-linear response surfaces characteristic of materials properties, such as the capacity in this work. Its non-parametric nature allows it to flexibly fit complex functional forms without requiring a priori assumptions about the underlying mathematical relationship. These characteristics, combined with its ability to provide reliable uncertainty quantification, make the RBF kernel the ideal choice for Bayesian Optimization and the active learning loop guided by our acquisition function.
The active learning method includes the following steps: data collection, feature engineering, machine learning model construction, next experimental points design, experimental test, and data feedback. The key point of active learning is to design the next experimental points according to the predicted value and prediction uncertainty of the machine learning model, and then iteratively optimize the next modeling by the feedback of experimental results until the model prediction meets the requirements.

Specifically, we used the Expected Improvement (EI) as the acquisition function to guide the selection, which considers not only the probability of improvement but also the expected magnitude of improvement, is the widely used as utility function. The EI is calculated as follows:
EI(x)=(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)Φ(Z)+σ(x)φ(Z)
where, μ(x) and σ(x) are the predictive mean and predictive standard deviation, respectively, of the GPR model at pointx. f(x+) is the best value observed among all experiments conducted so far. ξ is a tuning parameter that governs the balance between exploitation and exploration, for which we adopted the recommended default value of 0.01. Z =(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)/σ(x). Φ() and φ() are the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) and the Probability Density Function (PDF) of the standard normal distribution, respectively.

## Paper

## Abstract

Sustainable batteries necessitate high-performance hard carbon negative electrodes derived from abundant biomass. However, realizing their full potential is significantly limited by the inherent diversity of biomass feedstocks, the intricate control over carbonization and resulting microstructures, and the complex interplay between processing, structure, and electrochemical performance. Here, we introduce “intelligent carbonization”, a strategy integrating programmable Joule heating (1000-2000 °C, 10-60 s) with machine learning to substantially accelerate the discovery and optimization of biomass-derived hard carbons. By mapping over 1000 synthetic pathways and decoding the multidimensional feature space, we reveal a performance-correlated factor that serves as a crucial predictor of capacity, complementing conventional graphitic descriptors (in-plane crystallite size/ interlayer spacing). By a minimal energy input (0.1 kWh g-1), our strategy converts biochar into advanced hard carbon delivering 369 mAh g-1 reversible capacity, high rate capability, and improved cycling stability (>5000 cycles at a specific current of 3 A g-1). This data-centric approach allows low-cost and intelligent manufacturing of diverse biomass resources into performance-unified hard carbon negative electrodes, thereby paving the way for practical and large-scale biomass valorization towards sustainable energy storage solutions.

---

## Introduction

With an annual global production exceeding 220 billion oven dry tonne (odt) (or 4500EJ)1, biomass stands as an exceptionally vast, renewable, and ubiquitous reservoir, offering considerable potential for carbon-neutral product development2-5. The conversion of biomass into sustainable hard carbon (HC) negative electrodes is critical for fast charging lithium-ion batteries and particularly industrializing sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), which target large-scale grid storage demanding vast material supply and costs below $50 per kWh6. This dual role in energy storage and resource valorization underscores the importance of HC in advancing both renewable energy technologies and sustainable industrial practices. However, the complex and variable nature of biomass precursors makes it difficult to produce HC with consistent and predictable properties7-9, typically scattering from 150-300 mAh g-1, posing a significant barrier to industrial-scale manufacturing. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of carbonization and the unclear structure-property relationship hinders the rational design of HC from diverse biomass resources. Addressing these fundamental challenges is key to unlocking the full potential of biomass in next-generation energy storage.

Conventionally, HCs are produced via a two-step carbonization: 1) a low-temperature pyrolysis (~700°C) to yield the biochar, and 2) a high-temperature carbonization10-15 (e.g., 1400–1500°C for >2 hours) to tailor the graphitic microstructure of biochar into HC. While the biochar is abundant and cheap, the simple pyrolysis leads to premature microstructures and unsatisfactory performance (<200 mAh g-1)16, 17 (Fig. 1a). The latter carbonization stage, crucial for forming HC, is notably energy-intensive and incurs significant carbon emissions. Importantly, after this prolonged carbonization, HCs possess a complex microstructure with randomly oriented graphitic microcrystals, amorphous regions, and nanopores18-20, leading to variations in microstructure and performance across different biomass sources. For example, the rigid, lignin-containing frameworks of wood21, 22 and bamboo23 tend to produce carbons with robust, hierarchical pore systems; In contrast, the highly crystalline and pure cellulose from cotton11 is more conducive to forming well-ordered graphitic domains, translating into differing electrochemical behaviors (134~300 mAh g-1)24, 25. Moreover, the convoluted evolution of multiple structural parameters—such as graphitic microcrystal size, interlayer spacing, and porosity—is inherent to conventional carbonization26-30, posing a profound challenge of elucidating their structure-performance relationships. Consequently, the development of HC has been largely confined to an empirical, trial-and-error paradigm. While targeted synthetic strategies have provided initial insights correlating structure with reversible capacity, a quantitative and predictive understanding remains elusive31. In sum, developing biomass-derived HCs is hindered by three major challenges: 1) the energy-intensive carbonization process; 2) biomass diversity and performance variations; and 3) complex process-structure-property correlations for understanding and rational design.

Accordingly, establishing a paradigm for efficient, predictable, and genuinely sustainable manufacturing of HC with consistent performance is critical to advancing SIB technology. Herein, by integrating energy-efficient programmable Joule heating32, 33 (PJH) with machine learning (ML), our intelligent carbonization strategy unveils a critical capacity descriptor that unlocks the sustainable production of consistent HC from diverse biomass (Fig. 1b). The centerpiece of our discovery is a performance-correlated factor (PCF), derived from X-ray diffraction (XRD) data, which critically supplements traditional metrics like La and d002, together enabling a predictive model with greater accuracy for electrochemical capacity. This allows us to yield digital HC (Dig-HC) that exhibits a capacity of 369 mAh g⁻¹ (at 0.2 C, 1 C=300 mA g-1), more than doubling the biochar’s capacity of 150 mAh g⁻¹ (Fig. 1c), while also showing strong rate performance (280 mAh g⁻¹ at 10 C) and >5000 cycle stability. Critically, this improvement is achieved by PJH synthesis in an exceptionally energy-efficient manner34, consuming merely 0.1 kWh g-1 of electrical energy (~6% compared to biochar production). Our approach enables the production of a sustainable and high-performing Dig-HC from low cost biochar with an estimated production cost of ~$6,000 per ton—less than reported HCs (Fig. 1d). Leveraging this strategy, we demonstrate a full life sustainability pathway for HC negative electrodes: from renewable biomass, through an energy-efficient electrified carbonization process, to a durable high-performance HC negative electrode that enables a more resilient and sustainable energy future.

---

## Results

Synthesis and process optimization guided by machine learning.
While ML holds significant promise for materials science35-37, its application to HCs has been constrained by the bottleneck of slow, traditional experimental data acquisition. Specifically, while the initial synthesis of biochar from biomass via low temperature pyrolysis (T1: 600-800 °C, t1: 1-2 h) (Supplementary Fig. 1) is a rapid, high-throughput, and energetically favorable process, its conversion into HC is hampered by a lengthy and energy-intensive high-temperature carbonization (1400-1600 °C) that requires over 500 minutes. Our PJH carbonization strategy circumvents this limitation and completes the transformation from biochar to HC in under one minute (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Table 1). Compared to conventional carbonization, our method reduces the processing time by 500 times while requiring only 0.1 kWh g-1 of the energy input (Fig. 2b), with the detailed calculation shown in Supplementary Note 1. Despite the sub-minute processing time, XRD analysis confirmed that this rapid synthesis method does not sacrifice structural quality (Fig. 2c). The PJH treatment was sufficient to increase the in-plane crystallite size (La) from 2.184 to 2.64 nm while its transient nature effectively preserves a favorable interlayer spacing (0.371 nm) (d002) (conventional carbonization is 0.361 nm) and stacking height (Lc) a structural outcome that is beneficial for rapid Na⁺ intercalation and high rate performances38.

The four heating parameters create a vast design space (T1: 300-900 °C; t1: 60-120 min; T2: 1000-2200 °C; t2: 1-60 s) wherein material performance is highly sensitive to process variations, resulting in a diverse range of performances: e.g., capacity 100-300 mAh g-1, initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) 30-80% (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 2). Therefore, a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model coupled with an active learning strategy using an Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function39-41 (Supplementary Fig. 3) was applied to accelerate optimization of capacity and ICE of Dig-HC under four process parameters: pyrolysis (T1, t1) and PJH carbonization (T2, t2). Our initial analysis revealed moderate and comparable linear correlations for all four process parameters, while a strong linear correlation (R = 0.94) was identified between ICE and capacity (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 4). This simplifies our approach, whereby the dual-objective optimization was reformulated into a more parsimonious single-objective problem targeting only capacity. Our predictive surrogate model yielded a training R2 of 0.96, demonstrating its high fidelity in representing the performance landscape defined by the chosen data (Fig. 2f).

Our optimization strategy commenced with an analysis of the initial dataset, which identified that the PJH carbonization conditions of T2 >1800 °C are associated with higher capacity in our dataset. We initially fixed the PJH carbonization parameter (T2=1800 ℃; t2=40 s) to focus on optimizing the pyrolysis conditions (T1 and t1) (Supplementary Fig. 5). Upon mapping the parameter space (T1; t1) with the GPR model, we identified T₁=800 °C and t₁=1.5 h as the optimal condition for pyrolysis, considering its higher predicted capacity, lower energy consumption, and alignment with findings in the literatures11, 42, 43. Following T1, t1 determination, the PJH process parameters T2 and t2 were identified as an optimal second-stage temperature (T₂) of 1800 °C and the PJH duration (t2) of 40 s (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Fig. 6). After one iteration, the final model’s R² remains above 0.9, showing the stability of GPR model. The whole parameter space spanned pyrolysis and PJH carbonization, with predictions across 1,453 generated parameter combinations within this extensive matrix (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 7) facilitating later ML-guided optimization and intelligent manufacturing.

Electrochemical properties
To elucidate the advantages of our ML-guided intelligent carbonization, the resulting Dig-HC was compared against biochar and commercial Kuraray HC, showing higher sodium storage capabilities over the reference carbon negative electrodes. In initial charge-discharge cycles in ester-based electrolytes (Fig. 3a), Dig-HC achieved a high reversible capacity of 369 mAh g-1 and an ICE of 79%, exceeding precursor biochar (150 mAh g-1, 35% ICE) and commercial Kuraray HC (290 mAh g-1, 75% ICE)44, 45. To intuitively analyze the origins of its enhanced capacity, we performed a segmental analysis of the discharge profile (Fig. 3b), which revealed a dominant capacity contribution from the intermediate voltage stage in Dig-HC, delivering a 233.58 mAh g⁻¹. Furthermore, Dig-HC maintains 94.3% capacity retention at 0.2 C after 100 cycles (Fig. 3c), comparing favourably with Kuraray HC and biochar. According to the Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) profiles in Fig. 3d, Dig-HC exhibited a lower charge-transfer resistance (Rct) of only 23.67 Ω than that of biochar (52.24 Ω) and Kuraray HC (29.98 Ω), indicating an improved diffusion kinetics of Na ions (Supplementary Fig. 8, Supplementary Table 3). Additionally, the Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) analysis shows that Dig-HC has a larger integrated area, indicating a higher reversible capacity, as well as increased peak currents, which correspond to faster reaction kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 9).

The rate capability of Dig-HC was tested in an ether-based electrolyte to assess its performance robustness across different electrolyte systems. Fig. 3e summarizes Dig-HC alongside biochar, Kuraray HC, and representative literatures31, 42, 44-48 HCs under different specific currents. Dig-HC delivers 350 mAh g-1 at 0.2 C and 280 mAh g-1 at 10 C, surpassing biochar, Kuraray HC (Supplementary Table 4). Moreover, in the more challenging carbonate-based electrolyte system, Dig‑HC delivered ~80 mAh g-1 at 10 C—higher than biochar and Kuraray HC (<50 mAh g-1) (Supplementary Fig. 10). This further demonstrates the broad electrolyte-system compatibility of Dig‑HC enabled by our intelligent carbonization strategy. It clearly demonstrates that the contribution from fast, surface-controlled capacitive processes progressively increases from 45% at 0.1 mV s-1 to a dominant 72% at 1.0 mV s-1. This increasing dominance of non-diffusion-limited capacitive charge storage is the fundamental reason for the material’s strong high-rate performance (Supplementary Fig. 11). Regarding low-temperature performance, Dig-HC stabilized at 235.3 mAh g-1 and retained 97% of this capacity after 100 cycles at -40℃. It surpassed Kuraray HC, which delivered a capacity of 225.7 mAh g-1 before it short-circuited at the 17th cycle under identical conditions (Fig. 3f). Overall, Dig-HC demonstrated a robust electrochemical performance across a wide temperature range from -40 to 25°C (Supplementary Fig. 12). Even when the charging-discharging rate increased to 10 C, Dig-HC delivered 280 mAh g-1 and maintained 87.4% capacity retention after 5000 cycles, demonstrating enhanced stability relative to biochar (retained 62.4% after 4000 cycles) and Kuraray HC (short-circuited at 3000th) (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, when used as an negative electrode material in lithium‑ion batteries, Dig‑HC delivers a higher capacity (385 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g-1) than commercially reported graphite49 (372 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g-1). It also exhibits better rate capability, retaining approximately 141 mAh g−1 under a high specific current of 1 A g-1 (Supplementary Fig. 13).

Elucidation of structure-property relationships.
Despite achieving optimized Dig-HC performance, a comprehensive, predictive understanding of HC’s intricate structure-property relationships remains largely elusive. We selected XRD as the primary characterization tool, as it provides essential microstructural parameters (e.g., interlayer spacing d002, La, and Lc), with the detailed calculation shown in Supplementary Note 2, which are widely recognized as key factors influencing the performance of HCs (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 14). Moreover, the rapid, cost-effective, and highly reproducible nature of XRD makes it suited for generating the large datasets necessary to train a robust ML model and later industrial adoption. Conversely, techniques like high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) are ill-suited for large-scale feedback due to their localized sampling, complex preparation, and high operational costs. Moreover, relying on precursor characterization is infeasible, as the substantial evolution in phase and functional groups during carbonization severs the direct link between the starting material’s properties and the final negative electrode performance.

It should also be noted that the integrated areas of the (002) (i.e., A002) and (100) (i.e., A100) XRD peaks—which quantify c-axis stacking and in-plane graphitic order, respectively—are critical structural descriptors that are frequently ignored (Fig. 4b). Seven indices were chosen for subsequent analysis, including six physically meaningful features of d002, the interplanar spacing of the graphite (100) planes d100, Lₐ, Lc, A100, and A002 (Supplementary Table 5) and capacity. To bolster model robustness, extensive literature data on HC structural parameters were compiled (Supplementary Table 6) with our experimental data. Meanwhile, the range of both input structural indices and output capacities (Fig. 4c) is expansive, which underpins the development of a generalizable model capable of robustly identifying the optimal hard carbon structure.

By leveraging the automated feature extraction capabilities of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) (Supplementary Fig. 14), our model autonomously constructed four interaction features (A100/(A100+A002), N, A100+A002, and A100/A002) from the six primary descriptors, where A100/(A100+A002), named performance correlated factor (PCF), exhibits the strongest positive correlation with capacity (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 16,17). It reflects the relative contribution of in-plane ordering to the overall degree of order in HC (Supplementary Fig. 18). In other words, it serves as a mesoscale morphological descriptor rather than a direct crystallographic parameter50, 51. Built upon this enriched feature set, the surrogated predictive model demonstrated high accuracy, with R² values surpassing 0.94 on both the training and testing sets (Fig. 4e).

We then employed Shapley additive explanations52 (SHAP) to uncover the intricate, non-linear structure-property relationships within the MLP model, which reveals that the engineered feature, PCF, is the most dominant positive driver (Fig. 4f). It represents the fraction of in-plane graphitic ordering relative to the total crystalline content. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that a combination of a larger La and a smaller Lc is advantageous for Na⁺ storage, which is consistent with our linear correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. 19). It also clarified the nuanced role of d002, whose positive impact at a localized sweet spot (0.37-0.38 nm), thus reconciling our findings with the broader literature14, 20, 47. SHAP dependence plots (Supplementary Fig. 20) shows PCF and La have strong positive monotonic effects on predicted capacity, while d002 contributes positively within a narrow 0.37–0.39 nm window. Feature interactions indicate that enlarging d002 simply is ineffective, high capacity also demands a large La, and a high PCF. The PJH process notably co-optimizes PCF and La while pinning d002 in the optimal range, enabling the improved sodium storage.

To further corroborate the ML-elucidated structure-property relationships, a suite of additional characterization techniques was employed to compare Dig-HC and biochar samples (Supplementary Table 7, 8). While both samples displayed broad (002) and (100) graphitic carbon peaks in XRD, Dig-HC’s peaks were more intense and exhibited larger integrated areas53. Comparative analysis (Fig. 4g) showed Dig-HC possessed an increased PCF of 0.2 and a larger La of 2.64 nm relative to biochar, signifying a more ordered in-plane structure with larger graphitic domains. This structural enhancement is directly responsible for the increase in its plateau capacity, as it allows for more facile Na⁺ intercalation and pore-filling54. Critically, despite the intense thermal shock, the transient PJH treatment effectively preserved an interlayer spacing of 0.37-0.38 nm in Dig-HC, a range optimal for facilitating efficient Na⁺ intercalation55. Collectively, the intelligent carbonization strategy simultaneously promotes the lateral growth of short-range ordered graphitic domains (enhancing La and PCF) while suppressing their c-axis stacking (maintaining a larger d002 and a smaller Lc), a process wherein the curled edges of the microcrystals form abundant closed pores. These distinct structural attributes affirm that an engineered graphitic microcrystalline framework promotes high-performance sodium storage.

In addition, N2 adsorption-desorption analysis (Supplementary Fig. 21) revealed that the PJH process dramatically reduced the specific surface area (SSA) from 82.48 m2 g-1 for the biochar to 5.48 m2 g-1 for Dig-HC. This reduction is anticipated to curtail parasitic electrolyte reactions, thereby enhancing ICE and reversibility25. Concurrently, the average open pore diameters of biochar and Dig-HC are 2.2 nm and 9.14 nm, respectively. This observation is likely ascribed to the metastable, kinetically-dominated PJH process (< 1 min at ultrahigh temperature). During the rapid heating ramp Lc initially decreased (from 1.05 to 0.75 nm), while a 40 s dwell at peak temperature promoted recrystallization and an increase in La (from 2.18 to 2.64 nm). The subsequent rapid quench caused the thin, laterally large graphite microcrystalline platelets to curl, leading to the formation of larger closed pores. Together, these time-dependent kinetic effects during PJH explain the observed evolution of microstructure and porosity38, 56. Similar rapid synthesis techniques likewise show that employing rapid heating and cooling profiles can produce hard carbon with fewer defects and a richer, more diversified pore structure56. Further Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS)analysis (Supplementary Fig. 22, 23) elucidated a distinct shoulder in the scattering profile of Dig-HC (the scattering vector (q) range of 0.1-0.4 Å⁻¹, absent in biochar). This indicates the formation of larger, more well-defined closed pores, with the average size increasing from ~0.67 nm to 4.15 nm (Fig. 4h). Such developed closed porosity is believed to facilitate Na cluster formation, contributing to the low-voltage plateau capacity and concurrently bolstering ICE. Meanwhile, the first-cycle CV curves further indicate that this structure is more compatible with ether-based electrolytes than with ester-based ones , exhibiting sharper and higher peak currents and fewer side reactions, which facilitate the formation of a stable solid electrolyte interphase (Supplementary Fig. 24). Although morphological analysis by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) indicated no discernible differences among the three samples (Supplementary Fig. 25), HRTEM provided direct visual evidence for the structural evolution from biochar to Dig-HC (Fig. 4i, 4j, Supplementary Fig. 26). Dig-HC exhibited a more ordered graphitic microcrystalline architecture and a distinct internal porosity, indicating a higher degree of local graphitic ordering. Compared to biochar, Dig-HC possesses larger enclosed nanopores formed by the curling of short-range ordered graphitic micro-crystallites.

Raman spectroscopy57 (Supplementary Fig. 27) indicated that higher PJH temperatures lead to both a slight decrease in the ID/IG ratio (enhanced ordering) and an increase in capacity. According to the X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) results (Supplementary Table 9), C 1s spectra for Dig-HC revealed a higher proportion of C=C bonds (~284.8 eV), while O 1s spectra showed decreased C=O content (~532.3 eV) (Supplementary Fig. 28). This latter observation signifies effective impurity removal and suggests an increased sp3-carbon proportion as well as a more ordered carbon structure, which is considered beneficial for Na storage58. These results are consistent with the XRD and Raman data, further demonstrating the important role of PCF parameters for the enhanced battery performance.

Practicality and Outlook.
An intelligent manufacturing process (Fig. 5a, Supplementary Table 10, Supplementary Fig. 29) is proposed for highly efficient production of Dig-HC with high performance in real time based on the combination of the transient PJH method, the in-situ XRD characterization, and ML algorithm. In this workflow, the sub-minute (<1 min) PJH platform performs high-throughput synthesis. Concurrently, in-situ XRD extracts key structural features (e.g., PCF, La, d002). Based on our pre-established process-structure-property model, the ML algorithm uses these features to predict battery’s performance, perform inverse design, and generate recommendations for optimal process parameters. These recommendations are immediately fed back to the PJH process, enabling precise and rapid tuning of the HC’s structural features to meet target performance. Ultimately, this intelligent production approach not only replaces labor-intensive battery assembly and testing with rapid, data-driven XRD analysis and ML prediction but also establishes an efficient paradigm for the intelligent manufacturing of advanced HC negative electrodes with consistent and stable performance (Fig. 5b). Dig-HC not only shows enhanced performance than the conventional HC (Con-HC) in terms of capacity, rate, and cycling, but also achieves substantial gains in energy and time efficiency with a much smaller carbon footprint59. We used COMSOL Multiphysics to simulate the temperature distribution of a 100 cm × 60 cm heated substrate. The central processing region exhibits a highly uniform temperature field (Supplementary Fig. 30, Supplementary Table 11), consistent with the stable material quality observed at scale (Supplementary Fig. 31).

The adaptive control feature of our intelligent manufacturing process can be engineered to address the diversity of biomass precursors. For example, despite the profound structural differences between precursors—ranging from highly crystalline cotton (90% cellulose) and complex lignocellulosic peanut shells (45% cellulose) to glucose—our intelligent manufacturing successfully identified a robust optimization route for each, yielding HC capacities in the range of 340-370 mAh g⁻¹ (at 0.2 C) (Fig. 5c). On the other hand, our strategy can effectively achieve product and performance uniformity even from heterogeneous feedstocks. By manipulating the PJH parameters independently, Dig-HCs derived from the three above precursors exhibit a similar microstructure, evidenced by a convergence in their PCF from XRD analysis (Supplementary Fig. 32). As a result, our optimization strategy can consistently deliver consistent and high-capacity HCs stabilized at 340 mAh g-1, regardless of precursor origin (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Table 12). Furthermore, when substituting the input variables with the fundamental lignocellulosic ratios (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin), our intelligent carbonization strategy successfully converts these diverse compositions into performance-unified HC negative electrodes (330 mAh g-1) through iterative optimization (Supplementary Table 13, Supplementary Fig. 33). Significantly, the intelligent carbonization establishes a transferable paradigm for materials discovery. By leveraging transfer learning60 to freeze universal structure-property layers, the model can be rapidly adapted to updated multi-ion systems with minimal experimental data, enabling the efficient inverse design of bespoke materials for next-generation energy storage.

We performed a comprehensive techno-economic analysis (TEA) and life cycle assessment (LCA) of our intelligent carbonization strategy (Fig. 5e, 5f, Supplementary Table 14). Detailed analysis procedures, assumptions, and input parameters are described in Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Note 4. Specifically, our strategy reduces the carbon footprint from the carbonization stage by a factor of 14 and the overall costs by a factor of 30 relative to conventional carbonization. This leads to a 16-fold reduction in overall lifecycle emissions and an 8-fold reduction in total development cost, establishing a scalable blueprint where improved performance is achieved in concert with, not at the expense of, economic and ecological sustainability. From a life-cycle perspective, we establish a holistic and sustainable life cycle for advanced HC from biomass (Fig. 5g). The cycle starts with abundant and renewable biomass, which serves as a carbon-neutral and sustainable feedstock. This raw material is then transformed via our intelligent carbonization strategy, where energy-efficient and electrified PJH33 is guided by ML to minimize energy waste and consumption in producing high-performance and low-cost HC negative electrodes. The resulting HC then enables durable and long-life SIBs for sustainable energy storage applications. This sustainable cycle consists of renewable materials, electrified synthesis, and clean energy storage, representing a holistic, full-lifecycle approach to sustainable energy technology.

## Methods

Chemical and materials.
Cellulose powder (97%, ≤25 μm, Innochem, A06413, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ) was used as precursor. Cotton (degreased absorbent cotton; Labshark; purity 99%), peanut shells (purchased from Tan’ernuo; purity 90%), and glucose (Macklin; purity 98%) were used as biomass precursors. Acetylene black, polyvinylidene fluoride (Solef, PVDF 5130, DP = (1.0-1.2) × 106), Cu collector (purity ≥ 99.9%, thickness 9 μm) and CR2032 cell cases were acquired from Shenzhen Ke Jing Zhi Da Technology Co., Ltd. N-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP, purity ≥ 99%) were purchased from Aladdin. Organic electrolyte (ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate (EC/DMC = 1:1 by volume) or diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DIGLYME)) were purchased from DoDoChem. All reagents were used as received without further purification.

Material preparation.
All HC samples were prepared from cellulose pyrolysis (Innochem, microcrystalline powder) or complex biomass precursors (cotton, peanut shell, glucose) in two steps. Both steps of the heat treatment were conducted in an argon atmosphere. During the first stage of pyrolysis in a tubular furnace, cellulose powder was heated from room temperature to 800 °C at a rate of 5 °C min-1 and held at 800 °C (T1) for 90 minutes (t1) before cooling naturally to room temperature to form biochar. In the second step, PJH carbonization was performed using the programmable Joule heating method, rapidly heating to 1800 °C (T2) within 1 second and maintaining it for 20 s (t2), repeating this operation once. The HC material obtained by this method was named Dig-HC.

Materials characterization.
Scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30) were used to obtain information on microstructure. The phase was identified by XRD-7000 (Shimadzu, Japan) with a scanning rate of 10 ° min-1 (Cu K radiation, λ =1.5406 Å). Raman spectra were obtained by a WITEC alpha-300R, Germany. Pore distribution was tested by Xeuss 3.0 UHR, Xenocs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) was employed to analyze the chemical state of C, O and N.

Electrochemical measurements.
The negative electrode slurry was prepared by mixing 80 wt.% active material (Dig-HC) with 10 wt% acetylene black (Denka black, Denki Kagaku Kogyo; Average particle size was 20-40 nm) and 10 wt.% PVDF in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). The amount of NMP was fixed at 5 μL per mg of active material (e.g., 400 μL NMP for 80 mg active material). The mixture was stirred for 12 h at 26 ± 1 °C, and the resulting slurry was coated onto a single-sided copper foil current collector (purity 99.9%, thickness 9 μm) using an automatic coating machine. The prepared electrodes were dried overnight under vacuum at 120°C. The subsequent product was then cut into electrode sheets with a diameter of 12 mm using a disk cutter (Shenzhen Kejing, MSK-T10), and the loading mass of the active material was approximately 1-2 mg cm-2. A 0.4 mm sodium metal (diameter 14 mm, DoDoChem, stored in an Ar-filled glovebox (H2O and O2 levels both < 0.01 ppm) for no longer than one month before use) as the counter electrode and glass fiber (Whatman GF/A CAT. No.1820-090, diameter 16 mm, thickness 260 μm, pore size 1.6 μm, porosity 40%) as the separator, within an argon-filled glove box. The 1 M NaPF6 solution in ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate (EC/DMC = 1:1 by volume) or diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DIGLYME) was used as the electrolyte, and the amount is 120 μL. Charge and discharge measurements were conducted in a climatic chamber (25 ± 0.5 °C) using a Neware multi-channel battery testing system (CS3104).

In cycling test, the cells were tested from 2 V to 0.004 V with a specific current of 0.2 C or 10 C. In the low-temperature half-cell test, the temperature was set to -20 °C or -40 ℃, while all other conditions remained unchanged. CV curves were obtained with a scan rate of 0.1 mV s-1. The potentiostatic EIS measurement was conducted using an electrochemical workstation (CS6, Corrtest, Wuhan) in the frequency range 0.1 Hz-100 kHz with a signal amplitude of 5 mV. A total of 50 points were collected within the test frequency range. A quasi-stationary potential was applied for 600 s before carrying out the EIS measurement.

Machine learning models.
To quantitatively map the synthesis-structure-property relationships of the hard carbon, we developed a suite of machine learning models. First, a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model was established to predict the final specific capacity directly from four heating process parameters (designated T1, t1, T2, and t2). In parallel, a MLP, incorporating Dropout and L2 regularization and optimized via grid search, was trained to model the link between six key structural parameters and specific capacity.

Our GPR model was constructed using a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel as the covariance function, a standard and robust choice for modeling smooth response surfaces. The specific kernel was set as kernel = 1.0 * RBF (length scale=1.0); The primary advantages of the RBF kernel are its versatility and smoothness. As a stationary kernel, it is highly effective at capturing the smooth, non-linear response surfaces characteristic of materials properties, such as the capacity in this work. Its non-parametric nature allows it to flexibly fit complex functional forms without requiring a priori assumptions about the underlying mathematical relationship.

Our optimization strategy uses a closed-loop active learning workflow that couples data acquisition, feature extraction and surrogate modelling with experimental validation. The key step is the choice of the next experimental candidate. To make this decision, the algorithm updates the surrogate after each measurement and uses both the predicted performance and its associated uncertainty to steer the search—prioritizing promising regions while still probing less-sampled areas where uncertainty is higher. To implement this, we utilized Bayesian Optimization coupled with an Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function. The EI metric is particularly effective for this dual-objective task as it simultaneously evaluates the probability of outperforming the current best result and the potential magnitude of that improvement. The EI is calculated as follows:

EI(x) = (μ(x) - f(x+)) Φ(Z) + σ(x) φ(Z) (1)

The strongly solvated Na ions undergo rapid carbonate ring-opening reactions upon contact with the hard carbon surface. Conversely, in ether-based electrolytes (e.g., DME), the loosely coordinated Na ions (the coordination number of Na+ with O atoms is 3.2) facilitate a progressive and efficient de-solvation mechanism (Fig. R9b). This promotes the formation of a thin, uniform, and inorganic-rich SEI. Such an interface effectively preserves pore accessibility, enabling rapid ion transport and maximizing low-voltage capacity utilization (Angew Chem Int Ed Engl, 2025, 64, e202425507).

Comment #7. XRD-derived PCF, Raman-derived I_D/I_G ratio, and XPS-measured C=C bond proportion all reflect the ordering degree of materials. Response: Thank you for your insightful questions. While XRD, Raman, and XPS all probe the degree of graphitic ordering, they operate at fundamentally different physical scales and sensitivities. It is a big challenge to establish the quantitative conversion relationship between them. The specific advantages and limitations are as follows.
1. XRD (PCF): It serves as a bulk characterization technique that provides statistically averaged structural information over a large sample volume (mm3 scale), mitigating bias from local heterogeneity (Energy & Environmental Science, 2024, 17, 8189-8197). Crucially, the PCF is a mesoscopic morphological descriptor. It captures the relative dominance of in-plane ordering (La) versus c-axis stacking (Lc), effectively describing the unique “large sheet, thin stack” morphology of PJH-treated carbon. It is less sensitive to the chemical states of surface functional groups compared to XPS, which is not important to the sodium storage (Fig. R13a).
2. Raman (ID/IG): Raman spectroscopy is exceptionally sensitive to short-range disorder and defects (e.g., edge sites, vacancies) via phonon vibration modes (μm scale). Furthermore, the ID/IG ratio often exhibits similarity in HCs (Energy & Environmental Science 2024, 17, 1387-1396), limiting its quantitative linearity for ML modeling (Fig. R13b).
3. XPS (C=C %): XPS provides precise quantitative analysis of chemical bonding states (e.g., sp2 vs. sp3) and heteroatom content. It is strictly a surface-sensitive technique (probing depth < 10 nm) (Adv Mater, 2025, e11632). Since sodium storage is primarily a bulk phenomenon occurring in internal pores and layers, surface chemistry alone cannot fully predict the capacity (Fig. R13c).
Establishing a mathematical conversion between these metrics is scientifically challenging because they measure fundamentally different physical phenomena: long-range lattice diffraction (XRD) vs. short-range phonon vibration (Raman) vs. surface photoelectron emission (XPS). However, these metrics are qualitatively consistent and mutually corroborating (Fig. R13). The PJH treatment leads to a simultaneous increase in the PCF (indicating extended in-plane order), a higher proportion of C=C bonds (indicating defect healing), and a slight decrease in the ID/IG ratio (indicating reduced disorder).
