Response: We appreciate this insightful and forward-looking question, yet relying on such “direct” features poses significant practical obstacles.
Limitations of direct material features: Precursor-specific traits, such as elemental composition or functional group distribution, are largely decoupled from the final electrochemical performance due to the profound structural reconstruction induced by high-temperature carbonization. As demonstrated in our work, the final performance is dictated by the specific process-structure interaction (i.e., the graphitic domains and pore structures formed during PJH) rather than the initial state of the biomass (Fig. R5a). Our previous work (Joule 2025, 9, 101812) demonstrated that, even for pure small-molecule compounds such as PTCDA, the XRD and FTIR spectra of the carbonized products differ markedly from those of their precursors (Fig. R5b-c). Different precursors can yield unified performance under optimized conditions, while the same precursor can yield vastly different results under different temperatures (Fig. R5d-g) (Energy Storage Materials 2025, 80, 104367) (ACS Nano, 2025, 19, 14829-14838). Consequently, constructing predictive models based directly on material characterization features is challenging and likely to produce inaccurate results.

Comment #4. Details of the active learning framework is also missing, for example, which covariance kernel was used, how many experiment feedback-active learning iterations were carried in this study, etc.
Response: We thank the reviewer for requesting these important model details. Our Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model was constructed using a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel as the covariance function, a standard and robust choice for modeling smooth response surfaces (Sci. Technol. Adv. Mater 2023, 24, 2). The specific kernel was set as kernel = 1.0 * RBF (length scale=1.0); The primary advantages of the RBF kernel are its versatility and smoothness. As a stationary kernel, it is highly effective at capturing the smooth, non-linear response surfaces characteristic of materials properties, such as the capacity in this work. Its non-parametric nature allows it to flexibly fit complex functional forms without requiring a priori assumptions about the underlying mathematical relationship. These characteristics, combined with its ability to provide reliable uncertainty quantification, make the RBF kernel the ideal choice for Bayesian Optimization and the active learning loop guided by our acquisition function.
The active learning method includes the following steps: data collection, feature engineering, machine learning model construction, next experimental points design, experimental test, and data feedback. The key point of active learning is to design the next experimental points according to the predicted value and prediction uncertainty of the machine learning model, and then iteratively optimize the next modeling by the feedback of experimental results until the model prediction meets the requirements.
Our active learning loop was designed to identify the optimal performance within a minimal number of experimental iterations (in this case, only one iterations). The critical step is the selection of the “next-best” experimental point. To achieve this, we employed a Bayesian Optimization sampling strategy, which evaluates the utility or acquisition function based on the model’s predicted mean value and prediction uncertainty to design the next experimental points. Specifically, we used the Expected Improvement (EI) as the acquisition function to guide the selection, which considers not only the probability of improvement but also the expected magnitude of improvement, is the widely used as utility function. The EI is calculated as follows:
EI(x)=(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)Φ(Z)+σ(x)φ(Z)
where, μ(x) and σ(x) are the predictive mean and predictive standard deviation, respectively, of the GPR model at pointx. f(x+) is the best value observed among all experiments conducted so far. ξ is a tuning parameter that governs the balance between exploitation and exploration, for which we adopted the recommended default value of 0.01. Z =(μ(x)− f(x+)−ξ)/σ(x). Φ() and φ() are the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) and the Probability Density Function (PDF) of the standard normal distribution, respectively.
In each iteration, we select the process parametersx* =argmaxEI(x) that maximize the EI value as the next point for experimental validation.
